performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
question: What does the piano keep doing when the voice pauses to ask a question?
intro: Mary Garden sings Verlaine’s rain-and-grief poem with Debussy at the piano in Paris in 1904. The song’s moving accompaniment and restrained vocal line are two different kinds of continuity: one keeps falling, while the other asks why the heart is troubled. This acoustic disc is a historical document, not a modern studio balance.

sections.label: A · Rain and inward grief
sections.mNote: Moving piano figures accompany the contrast between rain and inward grief.

sections.label: B · A freer question
sections.mNote: The more freely paced question approaches; timing is approximate.

sections.label: A′ · The flowing figure returns
sections.mNote: Opening motion resumes for the final stanza and postlude; approximate placement.

cues.title: Rain moves while the voice holds
cues.text: The piano opens with a quietly repeating figure; the voice enters in longer notes. Listen for the independence of those two motions. Debussy does not need the singer to imitate falling rain when the accompaniment is already keeping it in motion.
cues.evidence: Ariettes oubliées no.2, printed pp.12–17 (PDF4–9): https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/8/83/IMSLP14819-Debussy_-_Ariettes_oubli%C3%A9es_%28voice_and_piano%29.pdf. The report shows a quiet initial window followed by stronger sound from0:05; the exact vocal entrance is not fixed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The poem keeps its question
cues.text: Verlaine places rain in the town beside weeping in the heart, then asks why there is sorrow without betrayal. The song does not supply a story that resolves the question. Its persistent accompaniment lets the uncertainty continue.
cues.evidence: The French poem is printed in the opened voice-and-piano score, no.2, pp.12–17. This is a paraphrase of Verlaine’s text, not a claim about which word is sung at0:30.

cues.title: The question changes the pacing
cues.text: Near the poem’s direct question, the score asks for freer pacing and relaxes the rain figure into a different kind of accompaniment. Keep the opening motion in memory: its recovery will matter even though the singer’s question has not been answered.
cues.evidence: Score pp.15–16: Modéré, ad libitum at “Quoi! nulle trahison?”, then Revenez au1er Mouvement. Report: strong changes around0:58–1:04 and a quieter1:05 window; the placement is provisional, not word-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer is the pianist
cues.text: Garden and Debussy made this recording in Paris in 1904. Their names are not a later reconstruction from the sound: the archive attribution is corroborated by a BnF catalogue and a specialist discography. The surviving disc brings both musicians into the same small frame.
cues.evidence: BnF notice, subnotice6: https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb38388874b; The Record Collector, IRCC107 / G&T33449: https://www.therecordcollector.org/articles/HRSandIRCCdiscographies/internationalrecordcollectorsclub.php; IA metadata identifies Paris1904. The precise day and studio are not established.

cues.title: The accompaniment outlasts the words
cues.text: Follow the rippling figure into the close. The written piano postlude continues after the voice, allowing the song’s motion to subside without answering its question.
cues.evidence: Score p.17 shows the piano continuing after the final vocal phrase. Report: lower closing windows at2:00–2:05, then decay by2:10. This locates the closing region, not an exact vocal release.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The rain figure yields to a question
transitions.how: The first stanzas keep the accompaniment moving beneath the voice. At the direct question, Debussy allows freer pacing and changes the piano writing, briefly interrupting the sense of automatic continuation. The contrast belongs to the setting of the words: a question takes time that the earlier repeated figure seemed to measure.
transitions.evidence: Opened score pp.15–16, Modéré, ad libitum at “Quoi! nulle trahison?”; report0:58 and1:04 changes and the quieter1:05 window. The64s boundary estimates the region; it is not a syllable alignment.

transitions.title: The moving figure resumes without an answer
transitions.how: The score asks for the opening tempo again. The flowing piano figure returns around the final stanza, restoring the earlier continuity even though the poem has not found a reason for its grief. The accompaniment eventually remains alone, carrying the repeated motion into the postlude.
transitions.evidence: Score pp.16–17: Revenez au1er Mouvement and final stanza/postlude. The report’s strong1:22 change is used as an approximate return landmark; exact lyric synchronisation is not claimed.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
